title: Nothing Holy
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Here is a summary paragraph summarizing the main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk: The talk emphasizes the importance of embracing openness and humility in spiritual practice, particularly through seated meditation (zazen). By letting go of attachments and expectations, practitioners can cultivate awareness and presence, even when faced with challenges or difficulties. This approach is rooted in the teachings of Bodhidharma, who embodied a sense of curiosity and devotion, and encourages practitioners to explore their own path while embracing the unknown, rather than trying to pin down or define truth.

sentences.text: Tonight, I thought maybe start a little series of talks on some of the family stories of Zen.
Like all families, we have our stories.

One of the unique features of the Zen school is that they came up with the idea that the Buddha's teachings on awakening and the end of suffering could be expressed through brief stories—usually of some kind of meeting or some kind of contact, some kind of encounter.
Sometimes an encounter between a Zen master and a student.
But stories, which was kind of a new twist in the Buddhist tradition, to put so much faith and so much weight in stories, often stories that are quite short.
Out of this, we have practices informed by these stories of meeting or touching something.
For example, our practice of one to seven days of sitting and walking and chanting together as one body, called sesshin.
That word sesshin means touching the heart, touching the mind—so contact, meeting, meeting the heart, meeting the mind.
We say meditation retreat, but that's not really what it is; that's not really a meditation retreat.
In the act of meeting or making contact or being with something right there in that moment of meeting is what we need, and that there's nothing outside of that.
These stories of meeting became the famous Zen koan literature.

Some of us have studied with John and with other people in other places, but I think it would be useful to bring up a selection of the koans, partly just to understand a little more about our tradition, and some of the archetypal and apocryphal and colorful and sometimes bizarre stories that inform the style of practice.
In earlier Buddhism and other schools of Buddhism, they don't write these down.
The story of encounters between teachers and students are private or just as a matter of course, or not even emphasized.
We are very used to in our school a strong emphasis on private meetings with the teacher, but other schools don't emphasize that so much.
Some other schools of Buddhism emphasize study, like a class, lots and lots of classes.
Other schools emphasize preliminary practices.
Before you would do meditation, you would do a preliminary practice like one hundred thousand prostrations, which is a common preliminary practice.
So you'd probably be pretty steady in your Zen-do attendance if you had to do one hundred thousand prostrations before you were allowed to come.
We emphasize these encounters, these stories, these private and public meetings as a way of understanding how we're meeting our life.
In Zen, they started writing down collections of the story of a master; it wouldn't be exactly like a sort of scholarly story.
The finer points of their teaching would be a collection of stories.

They started collecting these stories about different masters, different teachers in China, starting in somewhere around the sixth or seventh century, for the years these stories were retold in talks just like this one probably, and collected and codified and polished up until about the eleventh century when they were written down in organized collections—organized collections of stories, of koans.
The stories became sort of official and standardized.
Another great aspect of the Zen school is we have, and this is true I suppose of all Buddhism in a way, a willingness to sort of hold opposites together, hold opposite ideas together.
On the one hand, Zen has the idea of spontaneity, right?
Iconoclastic, bizarre, surprising behavior from Zen teachers.
And yet, the Zen school also has incredibly thorough going orthodoxy and consistency and official ways to do things and say things.
These stories are like sort of orthodox versions of spontaneity in some way, which is in a way bothersome and in a way really helpful to us because that's part of where we're tripped up.
We always want something to be this or that.
This is really characteristic of American culture around emotion, I think.
Like happiness should be spontaneous, for instance.
If you're happy, you're not sad.
If you're sad, you're not happy.
Buddhism suggests that it's a little more nuanced than that.
You can train in happiness.
You can be sad and happy at the same time.
These stories have that quality too, I think, of either and not either or.
The three most famous collections of these Zen stories are called *The Blue Cliff Record*, *The Gateless Gate*, and *The Book of Serenity*.
Tonight, I'd like to speak on the first case from *The Blue Cliff Record*.
It's hard to really know how important the order is, but it seems likely that the first one, just like in our culture, has a certain pride of place and is especially important.
I got on to doing this because, sort of like out of desperation, about a month ago I had to come up with a talk really quick.
I told you about my adventure in Massachusetts a couple of weeks ago, and so I just grabbed my favorite Zen story and gave me a little talk about it really quickly there, and it went well.
Then I gave the talk again here, and what I noticed was that different points came out in the talk.
I don't know if it was you guys in the audience or the situation, the meeting, or something different occurred to me, but a little bit different points came out.
Last Sunday, I gave the talk a third time in Seattle.
It's a well-shopped talk, but in the course of doing that, I was just sort of impressed anew by the depth and potential of these stories.
It's so easy when you read them to make certain assumptions based on your habitual view, and it's not all sort of spelled out.
It's not really explained; there's a lot of room to read things in or let things come out, or both.
So I thought it would be worthwhile for us to hear these stories and contemplate these stories.
Norman, at one point in his career, some of us probably remember this, set out a task for himself.
I'm not sure if I'm going to do this, but Norman at one point set out the task to give a talk on every one of the one hundred cases.
He was in a position, you know, he was coming up here, and I think still Abbott, maybe of Send Center, so he had a lot of opportunities to give talks, several a month.
He got through it in only a couple of years.
If I were to do it, it would take four or five years probably, but still, it might be worthwhile.
So who knows where we'll go, but we're on number one tonight.
I'm going to take a while.
One quality of these stories to mention up front is that these stories do emerge from a culture that shares some sexism with our culture.
Maybe we're a little better about this because it would even occur to me to say this is probably a good sign.
All these stories feature male teachers and students; very, very infrequently are women mentioned.
There is research going on as we speak, maybe right now.
Sue Moon and Florence are probably talking about their *Woman's Collins* book; this very evening they're making phone calls or something.
Research is being done into the women who were an important part of Zen history, Buddhist history.
Some stories are emerging that we will learn about, and some books are already out, so we should know that that's the case.
But I think it would be a mistake for us to be too worried about that point.
I think we need to be aware of it and do what we can to find out about the important stories that are centered about women.
But it would probably be a sort of a narrow feeling to sort of be mad at our uncles here because they forgot about our aunts, and our uncles and our grandfathers and our fathers.
Hopefully, we'll find out little by little about the women.
I just hope that we'll be open-minded and appreciate the dharma insight of these stories of our male lineage ancestors.
Not that there's anything wrong with being a little bit angry or a lot bit angry about this, but to hold our anger in a productive way.
Who knows how many thousands and millions of women were repressed in this time in eleventh-century China and all the ages before and after, and who knows how many men were oppressed.
Anyway, this particular book actually has two authors who are a century apart.
Time is a little bit different in these kinds of writings.
Oftentimes in the middle of the story it'll say later so-and-so asked so-and-so about this.
Sometimes that's like a hundred years later or a couple hundred years later.
We read that we think, oh, like, you know, an hour later, next day.
The first these hundred stories were initially collected in the early eleventh century to make this book by a Zen teacher named Shuedo.
Then later in the twelfth century, another author, another Zen teacher author named Yuan Wu, added commentaries and bundled it up and published a wood block book in 1125.
We actually know the date that it was published.
In a given story in here, there are words from both of these masters as well as the traditional story.
The first case is the famous story of Bodhidharma.
Emperor Wu of Liang asked the great master Bodhidharma, "What is the highest meaning of the holy truths?"
Bodhidharma said, "Empty, without holiness."
The emperor said, "Who is facing me?"
Bodhidharma replied, "The emperor did not understand."
After this, Bodhidharma crossed the Yangtze River and came to the kingdom of Wei.
Later, the emperor brought this up to Master Qi and asked him about it.
Master Qi asked, "Does your majesty know who this man is?"
The emperor said, "I don't know."
Master Qi said, "He is the Mahasatva Avalokiteshvara transmitting the Buddha mind seal."
The emperor felt regretful, so he wanted to send an emissary to go invite Bodhidharma to return.
Master Qi told him, "Your majesty, don't say that you will send someone to fetch him back.
Even if everyone in the whole country were to go after him, he still wouldn't return."
Bodhidharma, according to tradition, was an Indian monk.
Buddhism had already been in China for a couple hundred years, probably, sometime probably in the late fifth or early sixth century, something like that, maybe a little earlier, I forget right now.
But Bodhidharma is credited as being the one who set the tone for Zen in China.
The idea is that he is fresh off the boat, presumably.
For some reason, unexplained, he has an audience with the emperor of China.
The other part of the back story is that the emperor was a great patron of Buddhism.
Buddhism was one of the periods when Buddhism had state support in China.
By the way, that's a little bit funky when we make that Donna announcement when we say everything was freely given.
Sometimes it's like you're getting a big salary from the emperor, sometimes not.
Other times in China, the Buddhists were strung up and persecuted, thrown out.
I guess you never know.
I'm just waiting for President Obama to start supporting Zen.
For some reason, he gets an audience with the emperor who is himself a great patron of Buddhism.
Maybe you heard about this visiting monk from India.
India is the source country, just like we'd be excited if a Japanese Zen teacher was in town, probably, even if we don't know anything about him.
"Please come to our center and teach us."
I asked him, "What is the meaning of all this?
What's most important about Buddhism?"
Maybe there's a sense in this of a request for validation and support from this visiting holy person.
Bodhidharma doesn't give a discursive answer at all.
He doesn't explain anything; he doesn't try to help the emperor figure out how to practice, how to refine the system.
Bodhidharma doesn't ask for a salary himself, actually.
He just brings up the emptiness side of our life.
So much of our suffering is this mind that divides, that wants to be good, that wants to know what's the most important thing.
They use the word holy here in the English translation.
I don't know; I wasn't able to find out what the Chinese character being translated was.
You'll find out later.
For us, holy has a lot of connotations from the Judeo-Christian tradition.
So I looked it up in the dictionary, and for sure one of the meanings of holy is being close to God or in service of God, something like that.
But it turns out the word holy has actually an older root than that; it's older than Christianity.
The word holy has a root not in specialness or closeness to God, but it's from Old English and Old Norse for wholeness and completeness.
So holy is like whole.
That's another way we can look at this here: what is the meaning of the whole truth?
The whole of the truth.
We talked about emptiness a lot when we were studying the *Heart Sutra*, and here's just another way it's being brought up.
"There's no holiness.
There's no right and there's no wrong.
There's just this moment."
The emperor is a little surprised by this, and he asks Bodhidharma, "Who is facing me?"
Like, "Who are you?
What's your point of view?
What's your attitude?
What's your school?
What's your philosophy?"
That's maybe what he means there.

Here we have an interesting point: especially when this story is read, Bodhidharma is made out to be very, very strong, just sitting in his seat, unmoved by the sort of situation of being in the audience with the emperor of China, just putting his foot down.
I don't know.
Even it's understood like Bodhidharma is making a point or giving an emptiness teaching, like another level of emptiness teachings.
Not only is there no holiness, but we don't know who we are.
There is no me or you, you know, like with the emperor.
But I was thinking about it for this talk and I realized, well, we don't know that.
Maybe it's actually a very humble response, a very real and alive response.
Any Bodhidharma is a monk who is practicing diligently, trying to understand his mind and the patterns of how he gets caught in things and confused by things, the ways he forgets about emptiness.
And when he is asked this question, "Who are you?" he answers very honestly and very humbly, "I realized that any answer I were to give you wouldn't be quite right.
I can't say I'm me or this or that or the other thing."
And so it seems to me like the world is always asking us, "Who are you?
Who is this facing me?"
And we're in Bodhidharma's seat to some extent every day.
But in any case, the emperor didn't understand, Bodhidharma took off.
And then there's a second, there's sort of two halves here.
The second half is a conversation between the emperor and his advisor, Master Chi, or Chi, I'm not sure which.
And the thing that's interesting in that account, which on the face of it seems to be, "Whoops, Mr.
Emperor, you didn't notice, you had a really important teacher here.
He's gone, you're not going to get him back," but an interesting part of that exchange is the way that Master Chi praises Bodhidharma.
He says, "He is the Mahasatva Avalokiteshvara, transmitting the Buddha mind seal."
And so we know that the Mahasatva Avalokiteshvara, Kuan Yin here, is a bodhisattva of compassion and keeps showing up in emptiness texts, which seem to be about wisdom and discernment.
And here Bodhidharma has given this great, famous emptiness teaching: "All is empty, no holiness, I don't know who I am."
And the praise for that teaching was that it was compassionate.
So that's interesting.
The praise was compassion.
So wisdom and compassion are here in this story.
Then Bodhidharma famously goes off to a cave.
Eventually, nearby is the famous Shaolin monastery where they invented kung fu later and practiced really diligently.
So Bodhidharma is in addition to our exemplar for bringing up emptiness in the face of the world calling you forth to pin something down.
This is another way to look at that story, right?
The world is calling for you to pin yourself down, to give your position, to say how it is.
And so Bodhidharma is an example to us of the possibility of just openness, which is sometimes called for, and how quickly we try to pin things down.
So then he goes off to practice, and then he's ending his practice.
He's an exemplar to us of diligence, a very strong diligence.
So practicing all by himself, the story goes, he sat facing the wall for nine years.
One assumes he had to go to the bathroom and stuff, but you know, it's an example, it's a myth, right?
But it's a myth that we can bring forth that's helpful to us in our practice if we use it skillfully.
There's a great possibility to us for compassion, for softening around our story just from sitting still, just from devotion to the practice of quiet still sitting.
And there's all kinds of stories, myths about this.
It's such a central myth, so central myths spawn more myths.
And one of the funny ones is, they're all a little gross too.
They involve bodily mutilation to some extent.
So one of the funny ones is that he was getting a little sleepy, so he rips off his eyelids and tosses them out of the cave.
And where they fall is the first tea plants.
He's had tea to drink, help them stay awake, even though they can't fall asleep now with their eyelids ripped off.
So we don't really know if Bodhidharma actually existed.
There's evidence that he did, but some of it's a little bit shaky.
We certainly don't know if he...
There was an Emperor Wu, that's a historic fact, but we don't know if he met with an Indian monk.
And in a way that's a kind of a teaching of the story as well.
We have a fairly narrow band around what's real and valid.
So there's some encouragement here to receive some support from a somewhat bizarre, in ways, myth.
That's a root myth in a tradition that somehow, over thousands of years, brought us to this point.
So there's something to it, some energy there.

Another way that we can work with these cases, which I really recommend it's worth doing, is to read them over several times and just feel into what feels like the pivot point of the story, the sort of key point in the story.

And as these stories were further and further systematized, and training systems around them were systematized, especially starting in the sixteenth century in Japan, there's an official key point in every story.
But you don't need to worry about the official key point.
You can just see what feels most important in the story.
And oftentimes what people find about this particular story is this line, "I don't know."
It's written in the English translation as, "I don't know," with a personal pronoun, which is implied, I'm sure, in the Chinese.
But we can drop the personal pronoun, because who is it that doesn't know?
Anyway, just "don't know."
So this is one of the great things, I think, that Zen brings to modern discourse, the few nuts who practice it long enough to have some appreciation for it.
This "don't know," this not knowing.
That not knowing could be a positive thing.
It's kind of revolutionary, actually, quite radical, because we have a culture of knowing, right?
Of expertise, of degrees, of all kinds, certificates.
But there could be a great value, a great fluidity, a great freedom in embracing this not knowing, this "don't know."
And so it's actually possible to practice with this.
So let's do a little experiment.
So settle yourself in a little bit for a few moments of meditation, or whatever, stretch for a minute, or whatever you need to do to sit in there for a while.
We know that Bodhidharma, from his text, practices a lot with the breath.
We don't really know exactly how.

But let's take some inspiration from his example and just spend a few minutes really touching into the breath and the body, how the body actually feels at this moment, noticing that there's breathing, perhaps being interested in the feeling of the breath down low, the rising and falling of the abdomen.
It's a very grounded place, right in the center of the body, and really feeling the felt sensation of the breathing in the abdomen as the breath goes in and out of all the space that it needs.
You can count on the breath to do the breathing, the exhale experiment.

On each exhale, just inwardly drop this phrase, "don't know," giving some new energy in life and practices if the mind gets distracted, even with some commentary in this practice, just to bring it back to the intention, "breathing don't know," and then letting go of those words.
Return to quiet observation of the breathing and being curious about whether bringing up that "don't know" practice has generated some feeling of some kind, just to notice how things feel.
Thank you.
So it wouldn't be the worst thing to practice with that for a while if it caught your fancy.
And if it didn't particularly, that's fine as well.

But since Bodhidharma is also our inspiration for devoted zazen practice and is known to have worked with breath, I thought it wouldn't be the worst thing to mention a few ways that we often work with breath in zazen.
The first point about working with breath in zazen is that it's not an idea, it's actually a felt experience.
And it's interesting to sort of watch the mind.
It's very easy for breath to become the observation of breath become just kind of an idea.
So just to be curious, as you're studying breath always, is this really the felt sense of breathing in the body?
To notice it.
If it seems sort of always the same, it might just be the sort of idea of breathing, sort of degree of separation.
The mind is so good at generating sort of realities, right?
So that's the first point about breath awareness, to be feeling the felt sense of breath in the body.
The second point is that there are different ways of observing breathing.
And the first we often recommend is counting the breath.
And you may well know all this, I'm partly doing it for the recording, just to make sure everyone who practices, who listens to this stuff, will know these points because it's important.
And so the way that's done, and this turns out to be a very old practice, I was surprised to learn this.
I thought breath counting was probably invented in the nineteen sixty-eight because Americans were so squirrely or something like that.
But it turns out to be a very old Chinese written up in China in the era of these early commons.

And so the breath practice is to be especially attentive to the exhalations and mark each one with a number internally, starting with one, inhalation, then two, and then should one get to ten to return to one, or sometimes I say five is enough, turns out.
And if we don't get anywhere to return to one, if we get somewhere else to return to one.
And so what's nice about this is it gives us a very clear marker of whether we're actually attending to what's happening right now.
If we're not quite sure of the count, returning to one.
And that the important thing, too, is that one of the great things about breath counting is it activates our sort of aggression and competitiveness with ourself.
That we want to get to ten, because they told us go up to ten.
Never in any breath counting instruction that you ever hear did anyone ever tell you, "You should get to ten."
You made that part up.
It's interesting, huh?
So it's not about getting to ten, it's about attending to a clear kind of...
And then working with these ancillary states of mind, "Oh, I should be," "Oh, I failed," "Only made it this far," "Not doing too well tonight."
And it also helps us recognize that the state of mind is not like something we can sort of turn on and off with zazen.
The state of mind is conditioned by what's happening in our life.
And so the breath counting, instead of being a failure if there's a night when we can't get to two, it's just giving us information.
Like, "Oh, the mind is agitated, that's interesting.
The mind, the sort of internal weather is stormy."
And sometimes it's not even that obvious to us, you know, that we were agitated, you know, I'm like, "Oh, I guess there's agitation in the mind."
Sometimes it's really obvious, right?
Terrible things happen all day and, you know, no wonder.
So that's one thing that's nice about breath counting.
Another thing that's nice about breath counting is that return to one is a fairly clear and discreet inner.
We know, so that's nice too.
And so we can work with the quality of return.
How do we return to one?
Many different ways, gentleness or judgment or automatic, what would it be, automaticity?
Is that the word?
Automaticness or deliberateness, consciousness or unconsciousness.
So there's many different qualities of returning to one.
And so that's kind of what's interesting about breath counting is that returning the qualities of that and working with the qualities of that.
And breath counting is also helpful if, even if we normally don't do it, sometimes we take it up if the mind is really scattered.
There is a mysterious way that zazen is helpful to us regardless of our subjective experience.
So always to mention that when we talk to people about zazen, it's not about having a nice subjective experience.
It's nice, you know.
There's nothing wrong with having a nice subjective experience.
But it seems to be helpful in our life, done regularly, even if it's like a disaster zone in there every time.
Most people find though, if they take a step back and they look at the process of their life, the ways they're responding to our life, what's actually happening?
Well, you know, "I've been making a big effort to sit zazen thirty minutes a day and it always feels like I'm doing it wrong, but I'm way less.
I feel like less reactive than usual or something.
I feel sort of more in my skin somehow, less upset by something."
So that's the usual first way of practicing with the breath in our school of zazen, the breath counting.
Anyone is not in a hurry to sort of get past it onto something else.
I practiced breath counting for at least ten or twelve years.
That's all I did.
And then when I went to Tassajara, I told the teacher there, "Boy, my breath counting just feels very sort of rigid, and automatic, and I feel like I'm trying to get good at it.
And it's like, you know, can I please do something else now?"
And she said, "Oh, try counting backwards."
So then for several more years, I started at ten and went down and, you know, did so at Tassajara for however many thousand hours of meditation you do at Tassajara.
So not to be in a hurry.
There's no way I'm trying to accomplish anything.
It's that returning.

I'm practicing, but should breath counting seem too mechanical or too heavy, or too much like pulling you out of your experience in some way, if it becomes about these numbers off to the side, like in the movies when they're doing these weird movie versions of computers?
Then it's fine, of course, fine to drop it.
The next way of practicing breath usually suggested is just following, and there are a couple of ways to follow the breath.
There are many ways.
One is just to stay with that emphasizing awareness of the exhalations, just feeling that exhalation, letting it go.
At the end, you're aware of the inhalation, but the exhalation is just right where you're at.
So that's one way.
Another way is feeling the sweep of the breathing, inhalation, exhalation, very even.
You could feel it just in the abdomen, or you could feel the breath moving through the whole body.
There's a real interesting possibility around making some choices here, being a little bit creative and deliberate in our practice, not just a habit, a practice habit.
Here's my Zazen habit: to make some choices as we sit down for this period or this month or this year, I'm going to try practicing this way, following the full sweep of breathing.
And it's a great thing to talk to people about in practice discussion in Dokusan, of course.

A third way of practicing is to allow your awareness of the breathing to have, this is a little bit hard to describe, to have your awareness of breathing have a feeling of curiosity and interest to it.
There's a way of turning up the light a little bit, making the breath a little more vivid.
So it's sort of deliberately bringing forth a great sense of really not knowing what breath is, right?
Don't know.
Sort of just a liveliness.
And you can do all these things in different combinations: a real lively sense of the exhalation in the belly, a lively sense of the full sweep of breathing.
Another way to work with the breathing is to bring a phrase into the breath, which we just tried, which is, in a way, using language, using concept.
Every word, because of language, has a certain resonance and feeling to us.
Just dropping that in there.
But it's also a way of holding and marking and exploring breath.
A phrase that they often recommend that you try first is to ask a question, because a question gives a real liveliness.
So one of the most common questions is, "What is it?" or "What is this?"
Just breathe with that.
"What is it?"
But not to let the question become disembodied.
To really breathe with that question, hold that question in the body.
Bodhidharma went on to practice in his cave.
He has only four disciples that we know about.
Interestingly, one of them is a woman, whose name I don't remember; I should find out.
The first disciple, according to tradition, had to really prove how serious he was.
Do you know this story?
No, this is more gross than the island story.
So this is the story of the second Zen ancestor, Huinen, who Bodhidharma didn't think he was too serious.
Thought he was a little too in his head or something like that.
And he was outside.
I guess the cave had a door by then.
He was outside the door, and in the winter, asking for teachings, and Bodhidharma ignores him or something.
I forget exactly how it goes; I didn't look it up for this talk.
But he's insisting and insisting, and Bodhidharma's ignoring him, and it's snowing more and more, and he's buried in the snow.
"Please, please take me."
And then finally, for some reason, he had a sword.
That part is really unclear; why would this monk have a sword?
And he uses the sword to chop up his arm, and then Bodhidharma opens his arm.
"You're still here?"
Must have had a tourniquet with him too, because he didn't bleed out.

These are very masculine, aggressive sounding myths, but to take from them something positive: to take from them devotion, to take from them love, to take from them a willingness to challenge ourselves a little bit.
So if our Zazen practice is getting a little sleepy or a little habitual, a little groggy, be willing to bring forth this spirit of, "This is a precious opportunity."
We have this evening of practice together in this place that we work so hard and pay all this money for.
To bring forth that spirit of Bodhidharma: "I'm going to sit still.
I'm going to really be with breath."
And if I forget, I'm going to gently return.
Of course, it's so easy for us to misunderstand these exemplars, these examples, and get all stiff and uptight, causing a lot of pain in our back and shoulders.
Luckily, your back and shoulders will let you know, or the opposite, right?
To sort of rebel, goof off.
So, we hold it with some wisdom and with some compassion for ourselves.
And we can feel into how these stories, these examples, are actually alive for us, for each of us.
For each of us, it will be different than it is for me.
It was different for me last time I studied this story.
It's always changing, just like the dialogue we talked about a couple of weeks ago about the stone bridge and the log bridge: how is that in our life?
There are many aspects of this story.
The first aspect is the emperor wanting to be special, wanting to be holy in some way.
Is there a part of us who is like Bodhidharma who doesn't give a witty Dharma talk?
You can imagine Bodhidharma could have said something really clever and been given this big temple in the capital, right?
And it probably occurred to him: "The emperor is really asking me this."
But somehow he brought forth this spirit of humility and not knowing.
So what is that for us?
This, I don't know.
I'm willing to sit here and admit that I don't know.

Feeling into that myself tonight, I really didn't want to give, for some reason, I'm just not in the mood of giving a talk, and I felt like I'm not going to be very funny or interesting, and they won't like me or something like that.
And yet, I don't know.
